content: Myocarditis is characterized by inflammation of the heart muscle (myocardium) accompanied by the destruction of heart muscle cells (myocellular necrosis). Experimental studies suggest that after a viral infection, autoimmune mechanisms may be triggered, leading to further inflammation and damage to the myocardium. However, the use of corticosteroids as immunosuppressive agents in this condition remains a topic of debate. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of using corticosteroids to treat acute or chronic viral myocarditis. A secondary goal was to identify the optimal dosing regimen for corticosteroid therapy. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, BIOSIS Previews, ISI Web of Science, LILACS, and several Chinese databases, covering studies up to December 2012. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication status. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared corticosteroid therapy with no treatment, placebo, supportive care, antiviral therapy, or conventional therapy. Trials that combined corticosteroids with other treatments were also included, regardless of blinding or publication status. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers. Results were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences (MDs), both with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Eight RCTs involving a total of 719 participants were included in this updated review. The included trials were small and of poor methodological quality. Viral detection was performed in 38% of participants, with 56% testing positive for viral presence. Mortality rates did not differ significantly between the corticosteroid and control groups (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.24). At follow-up periods of 1 to 3 months, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was higher in the corticosteroid group compared to the control group (MD 7.36%, 95% CI 4.94 to 9.79). However, there was considerable variability in the results. In two trials involving 200 children, corticosteroid treatment was associated with an improvement in LVEF (MD 9.00%, 95% CI 7.48 to 10.52). No significant effects were observed on New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class or left ventricular end-systolic diameter (LVESD). Levels of creatine phosphokinase (CPK) were reduced in the corticosteroid group compared to the control group (MD -104.00 U/L, 95% CI -115.18 to -92.82). Similarly, levels of the creatine kinase MB isoenzyme (CKMB) were lower in the corticosteroid group (MD -10.35 U/L, 95% CI -11.78 to -8.92). However, these findings were based on a small number of participants, limiting the strength of the evidence. Data on adverse events were insufficient. The authors concluded that in patients with viral myocarditis and reduced LVEF, corticosteroids do not appear to reduce mortality. While corticosteroids may improve cardiac function, the evidence is uncertain due to the low quality and small size of the included trials. High-quality, large-scale RCTs are needed to clarify the role of corticosteroids in the treatment of viral myocarditis. Future studies should also carefully assess potential adverse effects of corticosteroid therapy.
